title: Sorting with a Comparator
summary: Let List.sort do the work, and say what order you want with a Comparator.

steps.title: Java already knows how to sort

say.never: Writing a sort by hand teaches you how it works, but real code uses Java's own: `list.sort(...)`. It's O(n log n), much faster than O(n²) on big lists, and it's been tested by millions of programs. What it *can't* know is what order you want. You tell it with a **`Comparator`**: an object that looks at two items and says which comes first.
say.bit: Use `list.sort(comparator)`: O(n log n) and well tested. The **Comparator** says which of two items comes first.

say.never: The easy way to make one is `Comparator.comparingInt(...)`, given a method that pulls out a number. `Song::getSeconds` means "call `getSeconds()` on each song". That sorts shortest first. Add `.reversed()` for longest first. Remember `import java.util.Comparator;` at the top.
say.bit: `Comparator.comparingInt(Song::getSeconds)` sorts by that number, smallest first; `.reversed()` flips it.

say.never: Two songs the same length? Without a rule, either could come first. `.thenComparing(...)` adds a second rule that only matters when the first one ties. Here, songs the same length go in alphabetical order by title. Ties matter at a competition: everyone should get the *same* pick list from the same data.
say.bit: `.thenComparing(...)` adds a tie-breaker that is only used when the first rule ties.

say.never: `sort` changes the list it's called on. If someone handed you that list, they might not want it shuffled, and a list made with `List.of(...)` can't be changed at all: sorting it crashes. So make your own copy with `new ArrayList<>(...)` and sort that.
say.bit: `sort` changes the list in place, so copy with `new ArrayList<>(list)` first.

marks.label: a copy you're allowed to change

steps.title: In your lesson: Sorting with a Comparator

say.never: `rankings` copies the list, sorts the copy and returns it. The order: by `getScore`, highest first, then by `getTeam`, lowest first on a tie. Watch out: `.reversed()` flips *everything* before it, so put it right after the score rule, before you add the team-number tie-breaker. Use `thenComparingInt` for a number.
say.bit: Copy, then sort by score reversed, then by team number. Put `.reversed()` before the tie-breaker.
